name: Gum grafting

lead: Gum grafting is a periodontal surgery that places tissue, most often from the roof of the mouth, over exposed roots or at sites with thin gum. People get it to cover roots, make teeth look shorter and build a thicker, more even gumline.

Tissue from the palate, neighbouring gum or a donor matrix is positioned and sutured at the recession site and heals in place over roughly two to four weeks. Common types include pedicle grafts, free gingival grafts, subepithelial connective tissue grafts and acellular dermal matrix, and much current research looks at palatal donor-site healing.

paras: A periodontist performs it under local anaesthetic after assessing the cause of the recession. Healing takes about two to four weeks, with soft food and careful brushing around the site during that time.

The palate donor site can be sore while it heals, and its healing and discomfort are the subject of several trials. As with other gum surgery, soreness, sensitivity and swelling are expected. Treating the cause of recession, such as gum disease or brushing habits, is a separate step.

chain: Even gumline and less tooth length
angle.text: Gum grafts cover exposed roots and restore an even, fuller gumline, so teeth look shorter and the smile frame looks more balanced. The covered root is a visible result of the surgery, and outcomes by technique are widely studied.

lead: Gum grafting is a periodontal plastic surgery in which gum tissue, usually taken from the palate or from a donor source, is placed at a site with gum recession or too little keratinised tissue. For appearance it can cover exposed tooth roots that make teeth look long, even out an uneven gumline and thicken a thin gum band, and the procedure has been described in the dental literature as cosmetic gum grafting.[1][2][3]

Common types include pedicle grafts that move nearby tissue, free gingival grafts, subepithelial connective tissue grafts and acellular dermal matrix as an alternative to palate tissue.[4][3] Healing is reported to take about 2 to 4 weeks.[4] Much of the current research concerns palatal donor-site healing and keratinised tissue around implants.[5][6]

Wikipedia's article on the procedure notes that recession on front teeth can look unattractive in addition to causing sensitivity and exposing roots, and that grafts aim to restore protective tissue. It also notes that not every recession needs surgery.[3]

paras: A pedicle graft moves tissue next to the recession over the exposed root. A free gingival graft or subepithelial connective tissue graft uses tissue from the palate, and an acellular dermal matrix is a processed donated skin product used instead of the patient's own tissue.[4] A 1997 article described cosmetic gum grafting.[2]

Wikipedia's account of gingival grafting describes the free gingival graft as a thin layer of palatal tissue sutured over the recession, often used to thicken very thin gum. The subepithelial connective tissue graft takes tissue from beneath the palatal surface and is described as offering excellent predictability of root coverage with less palatal pain than a free graft. A lateral pedicle graft rotates tissue from beside the defect and needs enough adjacent tissue, and it can cause recession at the donor tooth.[3]

Other options listed there include acellular dermal matrix such as Alloderm, which avoids a palatal donor site although periodontists disagree on whether it matches connective tissue grafts, and allografts or xenografts from cadaver or animal sources. Coronally or apically positioned flaps move existing gum without adding new tissue, and advanced platelet-rich fibrin, associated with Joseph Choukroun, uses a centrifuged blood sample to make a growth-factor-rich clot placed over the recession so that no palatal harvest is required.[3]

Besides covering recessions, grafts are used where keratinised tissue is limited. A 2026 case study described placing a free gingival graft before a regenerative procedure at a site with limited keratinised tissue.[1] Registered trials also examine keratinised tissue augmentation and soft-tissue health around dental implants.[6][7][8]

In appearance terms, an 18-month registered trial compared a gingival unit graft with a free gingival graft using digital colour analysis, reflecting interest in how well the grafted tissue blends with the surrounding gum.[9]

Healing is reported to take about 2 to 4 weeks.[4] Wikipedia's grafting article reports that, according to a 2018 review of root coverage procedures, most procedures reduced recession, and that discomfort came mostly from the harvest site, usually in the first week, without affecting root coverage outcomes.[3]

Registered trials compare a gingival unit graft with a free gingival graft over 18 months,[9] test wound-healing products and techniques at the palatal donor site,[10][11][12] examine keratinised mucosa and soft-tissue health around implants,[7][8] examine shrinkage of reharvested grafts,[5] and compare graft harvesting techniques in recession sites.[13] Published results are not summarised here. Published clinical reports include a case study.[1]
A 2018 review summarised on Wikipedia found that most root coverage procedures reduced gum recession.[3]

Palatal donor-site wound healing, pain and comfort are themselves the subject of trials, indicating the donor site is a recognised source of morbidity.[10][11] Wikipedia lists limited donor tissue and donor-site morbidity for palatal harvesting, possible poor healing and disease-transmission risk with allografts, and recession at the donor site with pedicle grafts.[3]
